analysis.successDefinition: All four functional fixes (providers-filter guard, maxBodyBytes cap, streamed-request-body wait, synthetic getHeader truth) and the packaging hygiene bundle ship on a single coherent 0.2.1 patch; every fix has a real test (the missing negative fetch test for non-provider hosts, a deterministic race/concurrency test for the request-body wait, a header-correctness test for the synthetic getHeader fix, a cap-trip test, packaging-sanity tests for the metadata/lockfile/VERSION/shim/exports issues); tsc, eslint, and jest stay green throughout the horizon; `npm pack --dry-run` shows a clean tarball without sdk-fetch-shim and without a duplicate lockfile; `arethetypeswrong` no longer flags the .d.ts types condition; the generated VERSION constant matches package.json's 0.2.1.
assumptions: The line numbers cited in the brief for packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts (258–260, 267, 280–298, 833, 854, 882) are accurate and the described bug shapes match the current code (discovery confirmed 258-260, 267, 833, 854, 882; corrected the race range to 302-396).

Jest 29 + ts-jest is the test framework (discovery corrected the brief's Vitest assumption), and the existing `providers: [/127\.0\.0\.1|localhost/]` test pattern is the right baseline for tests that DO want capture.

tsc already produces both dist/esm and dist/cjs; adding a separate `dist/esm/index.d.ts` types condition does not require introducing a new bundler, only verifying tsconfig emits declarations for both.
The agreed target version is 0.2.1, and the single source of truth is package.json — VERSION is generated at build time from `pkg.version`, never hand-duplicated.

For the patch-stacking interaction, 'document the limitation at minimum' is the agreed floor; a clearer restoration signal is best-effort and is only included if its diff is small and reviewable in the same horizon — kept for the next horizon via the Planning Brief.

pnpm is the surviving lockfile: the monorepo layout (packages/elenwatch) implies pnpm-workspace usage, so pnpm-lock.yaml stays and package-lock.json is removed (with a clear note in the commit/README that this repo is pnpm-managed).
CI is added in the next horizon (deferred), not this one; this horizon ships a working 0.2.1 functionally and the next horizon wraps it in GitHub Actions.

maxBodyBytes is a defense-in-depth safety net rather than the primary privacy boundary: the default is set high enough not to clip realistic LLM payloads (≈10 MiB) but low enough to bound memory exposure, and a clear log line is emitted when the cap trips.

Removing sdk-fetch-shim from the dist tree (rather than repairing its @ai-sdk/anthropic deep import type) is the right call because the shim is test-only and unexported — deep imports stop working by design.
This is a patch release: documented public exports (namedElenwatchWatch, install, restore, etc.) and their signatures are unchanged; only internal behavior and packaging metadata move.

The synthetic getHeader fix only needs to be correct for the keys elenwatch itself reads (host, content-length, content-type, transfer-encoding) — a fully populated synthetic header map is YAGNI for the present horizon.

The unused-eslint-disable verification in otel.ts:38 and otel.test.ts:101 may find one or both directives are actually load-bearing under the type-aware rule set (tseslint.configs.recommendedTypeChecked) — keep the directive if lint fails after removal.
risks: The streamed-request-body race test is timing-sensitive if not built carefully: Node chunk ordering, backpressure, and undici's internal scheduling can make a 'before fix' test flaky. Mitigation: deterministic slow-upload fixture (a transform stream that releases one chunk per microtask) plus an ordering check by code inspection or by intercepting dispatch with a spy, not by waiting.

The synthetic getHeader fix is a contract change: any code that today reads a non-host header from the synthetic request (e.g., assuming `getHeader('content-length')` returns a number) silently gets undefined after the fix. The host-fallback dimension's passCriteria guards the only in-file consumers (deriveUrl and reqHostname, both reading `host`).

maxBodyBytes default value is a real tuning risk: too low (e.g., 1 MiB) clips real LLM request payloads and causes false-positive 'body dropped' log noise; too high (e.g., 1 GiB) gives no memory protection. The default is ~10 MiB and the onBodyDropped callback gives operators a structured hook to react.

Removing package-lock.json from packages/elenwatch/ can break a contributor's local workflow if their editor or test runner cached it. Mitigation: .gitignore line is already present (confirmed by discovery), pnpm-lock.yaml is the surviving lockfile.

Build-time VERSION generation is a new build step; if it fails silently in CI, dist could ship with a stale VERSION constant. Mitigation: prebuild script in package.json's scripts, and a packaging-build.test.ts that reads built dist and asserts VERSION === package.json's version.

The patch-stacking interaction under dd-trace/newrelic is fundamentally unfixable in code: elenwatch cannot reliably peel another wrapper off `write`/`end` once those agents have stacked on top after `install()`. Documentation is the honest path; the next horizon carries the README Limitations section.

discoveryFindings.area: CRITICAL: providers-filter ignored on fetch/undici path
discoveryFindings.finding: Confirmed at packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts:267. The call site reads `this.interceptor.attachCapture(syntheticReq as unknown as ClientRequest, callerTrace)` and is unconditional — the surrounding dispatch() method never invokes shouldCapture(syntheticReq, this.interceptors.providers) before attaching. The http-patch path in the same file does check at lines 833 (onWrapper), 854 (writeWrapper), and 882 (endWrapper). The kNoCapture tag for the fetch path is never used today.
discoveryFindings.implication: The fix must (a) run shouldCapture(syntheticReq, this.providers) before attachCapture and (b) short-circuit — i.e. skip attachCapture AND skip the body-teeing branch at lines 286-398 entirely — when shouldCapture returns false. A new local `let shouldAttach = shouldCapture(syntheticReq, this.providers)` followed by an `if (!shouldAttach) { return this.original.dispatch(options, handler); }` early-return is the clean shape; the negative test must assert zero entries AND zero buffer allocation in the WrappingDispatcher's capture branch.

discoveryFindings.finding: The brief's cited range src/interceptor.ts:280-298 covers the COMMENT that documents the race plus the synchronous-body branches. The actual race-prone AsyncIterable teeing code lives at lines 302-396, specifically the second `void (async () => { ... })()` at lines 385-396.
discoveryFindings.implication: Cite the 302-396 range, not 280-298. A 'deterministic wait' means: in the capture branch (lines 385-396), instead of a fire-and-forget, the capture branch must `await` upstream completion BEFORE calling `this.original.dispatch(options, wrappedHandler)` — i.e. flip the order: capture-body first, dispatch second.

discoveryFindings.finding: Logger.ts defines `export type Logger = (entry: LlmLogEntry) => void` — the seam accepts only LlmLogEntry, with no separate 'body dropped' event channel. options.ts has no maxBodyBytes field on InterceptorOptions. phases.name: Add providers-filter guard on fetch path
phases.goal: Make the fetch/undici code path honor the user-supplied providers filter the same way the http/https patch path already does, so that requests to non-provider hosts never enter the capture pipeline.
phases.rationale: The fetch dispatch entry at packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts:267 calls attachCapture unconditionally. The http/https patch path checks shouldCapture and tags with kNoCapture when it returns false. The fetch path never calls shouldCapture, so the providers filter is silently bypassed for every fetch call. This is the critical fix — without it, every fetch() in the host process leaks to the logger and pins memory on responseBodyChunks.
changes: Compute `const shouldAttach = shouldCapture(syntheticReq, this.providers)` immediately before the existing `this.interceptor.attachCapture(...)` call at interceptor.ts:267.

Add an early-return `if (!shouldAttach) { return this.original.dispatch(options, handler); }` so the body-teeing branch at lines 286-398 is also skipped for non-provider hosts — no capture-state struct allocated, no body buffer held.

Add a negative fetch test in interceptor.test.ts (NOT in the integration file, so it runs in the default Jest suite) with `providers: [/api\\.openai\\.com/]` that fetches a 127.0.0.1 test server, flushes with setImmediate, and asserts (a) no LlmLogEntry is passed to logger and (b) no `responseBodyChunks` buffer exists on the capture-state struct.

phases.name: Change synthetic getHeader to return undefined when absent
phases.goal: Make the synthetic getHeader return undefined for any header key that is not present in the underlying header map, while preserving the host fallback for the `host` key only.
phases.rationale: The current implementation at interceptor.ts:258-260 falls back to hostHeader for any missing key, so a request that has no `content-length` silently returns a host-looking string instead of undefined. phases.name: Change request-body capture to await upstream completion
phases.goal: Make the streamed (AsyncIterable) request-body capture deterministic so the response handler's onComplete cannot fire before the full request body has been captured and emitted into the capture entry.
phases.rationale: The race-prone fire-and-forget at interceptor.ts:385-396 lets the dispatch call return and trigger onComplete while the capture branch is still mid-await on the shared waiter queue. The result is capture entries with partial or empty request bodies. The fix reorders capture-body-first then dispatch-second so onComplete cannot fire until capture is fully complete. Discovery found the actual race site is lines 302-396 (not 280-298 as the brief said).
changes: Refactor the AsyncIterable teeing block at interceptor.ts:302-396 so the capture promise is awaited BEFORE `this.original.dispatch(options, wrappedHandler)` is called.
Adapt the dispatch return type so callers (and the onComplete path) only fire after both capture and the original dispatch have settled.

Add a deterministic test fixture using a transform stream that releases exactly one chunk per microtask (so the upstream never completes synchronously), upload a multi-chunk body through fetch, and assert (a) the captured request body in the emitted LlmLogEntry equals the full uploaded body and (b) the capture emission ordering is deterministic by code inspection or by intercepting dispatch with a spy.

rubric.label: Capture completes before dispatch returns (source-level)
rubric.ruleStatement: In packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts every AsyncIterable body-capture branch must `await` the body-capture-completing promise in the same async frame as the call to `this.original?.dispatch(...)`. Sequencing must NOT rely on `setTimeout`, `setImmediate`, `queueMicrotask`, `Promise.resolve().then`, or any `sleep`-style yield between the capture-await and the dispatch call. Scale: 10 = a reviewer cannot find a single code path where onComplete can fire while capture is still pending; 8 = the one AsyncIterable branch is correctly sequenced and the sync non-iterable path is untouched; minScore 7.
passCriteria: Run `grep -nE 'this\.original(\?|\b)\.dispatch\(' packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts` and for every call site reached from the AsyncIterable teeing block, confirm an `await` on the capture-completing promise appears earlier in the same enclosing `async` function.

Run `grep -nE 'setTimeout|setImmediate|queueMicrotask|Promise\.resolve\(\)\.then|process\.nextTick' packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts` inside the body-capture / dispatch wrapper and confirm zero matches used to defer dispatch for sequencing reasons.

Inspect the `capture-state` struct (`capturedEnd`, `finished` fields) and confirm the promise that resolves the await is the one whose resolve is called only after the AsyncIterable has been fully drained.
Confirm the synchronous fast path for non-Iterable / non-streaming bodies still bypasses the teeing block.
failureExamples: Dev writes `await captureDone; this.original?.dispatch(opts, wrappedHandler);` correctly for the happy path, but in the `catch` arm of the teeing block calls dispatch synchronously — the upstream error path now bypasses capture-finalization.
Dev awaits the capture promise but then wraps dispatch in `Promise.resolve().then(() => dispatch(...))` — dispatch is now scheduled on a later microtask and onComplete can win the race.
Dev inserts `await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r))` between capture-await and dispatch to 'give the upstream room' — looks like it works, is timing-based, and will flake under load.

phases.name: Add maxBodyBytes cap with body-dropped event
phases.goal: Add a configurable byte cap on buffered request and response bodies as a defense-in-depth safety net, and emit a structured event when the cap trips.
phases.rationale: The current capture buffers every body chunk without bound (no byte accounting in the capture-state struct and no cap in appendChunk at lines 564-591), so a malicious or runaway provider can pin unbounded memory. The providers filter is the primary privacy boundary; maxBodyBytes is a secondary safety net. A separate `onBodyDropped` callback keeps the single-purpose Logger seam clean.
changes: Add `maxBodyBytes?: number` (default ~10 MiB) and `onBodyDropped?: (info: { host: string; direction: 'request' | 'response'; bytes: number; cap: number }) => void` to InterceptorOptions in options.ts and document both in the docstring at lines 78-111.

Plumb maxBodyBytes through the Interceptor constructor (interceptor.ts:683-692) into the capture-state struct; add per-direction `bytesCaptured: number` and `bodyDropped: boolean` to the capture-state struct on interceptor.ts:95-118.

Update appendChunk at interceptor.ts:564-591 to short-circuit further capture for a direction once `bytesCaptured + chunk.byteLength > maxBodyBytes`, set `bodyDropped = true`, and invoke the onBodyDropped callback exactly once with the structured info.
Emit a clear console message ('elenwatch: dropping body for host X, Y bytes exceeds maxBodyBytes Z') when the cap trips so operators can tune it.

Add a cap-trip test that uploads a request body exceeding maxBodyBytes (small cap, e.g. 256 bytes) and asserts no further body chunks are appended to requestBodyChunks AND the onBodyDropped callback is invoked exactly once with the expected info.
phases.boundedContext: Configuration (options + logger seam) and HTTP capture (interceptor)
inputs: InterceptorOptions shape at packages/elenwatch/src/options.ts lines 112-121
Logger type definition at packages/elenwatch/src/logger.ts lines 1-37
capture-state struct and appendChunk logic at packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts lines 95-118 and 564-591
Brief's chosen default (~10 MiB) and body-dropped seam design (parallel onBodyDropped callback)
phases.expectedResult: maxBodyBytes cap trips and emits body-dropped event; cap-trip test passes asserting no further capture and exactly one callback invocation

rubric.label: Cap-trip test asserts capture stops AND callback fires exactly once

A score of 10 means the test in packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.test.ts (a) constructs a request whose body exceeds a deliberately-small maxBodyBytes (≤1024 bytes), (b) asserts that no chunks after the trip are appended to requestBodyChunks, and (c) asserts that onBodyDropped is invoked exactly once with { host, direction: 'request', bytes >= cap, cap = maxBodyBytes }. minScore 7.
passCriteria: A test in interceptor.test.ts has a name containing 'maxBodyBytes' or both 'body' and 'cap'.
The test sets maxBodyBytes to a value ≤1024 and sends a request whose body.byteLength strictly exceeds that value.
The test reads requestBodyChunks after the request completes and asserts its total byteLength is ≤ maxBodyBytes (the cap).
The test installs a spy (jest.fn) on onBodyDropped and asserts `spy.mock.calls.length === 1`.
The test asserts the first callback argument has `direction === 'request'`, `cap === maxBodyBytes`, `bytes >= cap`, and `host` is the destination hostname.

Test asserts `spy.mock.calls.length >= 1` instead of `=== 1`.
Test uses a body whose size does not actually exceed the cap.
Dev wrote the request-side test but skipped a response-side test.

rubric.label: Cap accounting and short-circuit are per direction on the capture-state struct
rubric.ruleStatement: A score of 10 means the capture-state struct at packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts:95-118 carries `bytesCaptured: number` and `bodyDropped: boolean` independently for the request direction and for the response direction, appendChunk at interceptor.ts:564-591 short-circuits as soon as bytesCaptured[direction] + chunk.byteLength > maxBodyBytes, and both the request-body path and the response-body path consult the same per-direction fields. minScore 7.
passCriteria: The capture-state type in interceptor.ts declares two pairs of fields — one for request, one for response — for bytesCaptured and bodyDropped.
appendChunk contains an early-return guard `if (bodyDropped[direction]) return;` that runs BEFORE the buffer.push.
Chunk size is computed via Buffer.byteLength or new TextEncoder().encode(chunk).byteLength, never via string `.length`.
`grep -n 'bodyDropped' packages/elenwatch/src/interceptor.ts` returns at least two call sites — one in the request-body path and one in the response-body path.
When maxBodyBytes is undefined, appendChunk behaves identically to its pre-phase behavior.
failureExamples: Developer uses `requestBodyChunks.length` (chunk count) as the byte counter.
Developer stores a single `bodyDropped: boolean` shared between request and response.
appendChunk still pushes the chunk into the array but skips only the counter update after the push.
Developer computes chunk size with `chunk.length` on a string, missing that non-ASCII characters are multiple bytes.

rubric.label: onBodyDropped fires once per direction with the structured info object
rubric.ruleStatement: A score of 10 means onBodyDropped is invoked exactly once per (host, direction) on the first chunk whose append would exceed maxBodyBytes, with payload { host: string; direction: 'request' | 'response'; bytes: number; cap: number } where bytes is the running total at the moment of the trip. minScore 7.

The JSDoc block above the type names both new fields, says 'bytes' for the cap unit, and states the default value.
